questions.stem: Iron filings are heated with sulfur: Fe + S → FeS. What type of reaction is this?
questions.explanation: Two elements combine to form a single compound, which is a synthesis reaction. Decomposition is the reverse, one compound breaking into simpler substances.

questions.stem: Limestone is heated strongly: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What type of reaction is this?
questions.explanation: One reactant breaks down into two simpler products, so this is thermal decomposition. Combustion needs a fuel reacting with oxygen, and no oxygen is a reactant here.

questions.stem: What are the products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation: In a plentiful supply of oxygen, all the carbon in a hydrocarbon forms carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen forms water. Carbon monoxide and soot form only when oxygen is limited.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈?
questions.explanation: Three carbons give 3CO₂ and eight hydrogens give 4H₂O. That is 6 + 4 = 10 oxygen atoms on the right, so 5O₂ is needed. With only 3O₂ the oxygen does not balance.

questions.stem: Methane burns in a limited supply of oxygen. Which products can form?
options: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas only
questions.explanation: With too little oxygen, some carbon is only partly oxidised to carbon monoxide or left as soot, while the hydrogen still forms water. Carbon monoxide is toxic, which is why heaters need ventilation.

questions.stem: What are the products when sulfuric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: An acid and a hydroxide base react to form a salt and water: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) comes from sulfuric acid; sulfite is SO₃²⁻ and sulfide is S²⁻.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced equation for the reaction of hydrochloric acid with calcium carbonate?
questions.explanation: An acid and a carbonate form a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Calcium forms Ca²⁺, so the salt is CaCl₂, and two HCl are needed to balance the chlorine.

questions.stem: Which equation represents a decomposition reaction?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into two simpler substances, water and oxygen. The others are synthesis, neutralisation and displacement.

questions.stem: Which ions form compounds that are all soluble in water?
questions.explanation: Compounds of the group 1 ions, ammonium and nitrate are soluble. Silver, lead and barium form several insoluble salts, and most carbonates, phosphates and hydroxides are insoluble.

questions.stem: Which compound is insoluble in water?
questions.explanation: Most sulfates dissolve, but barium sulfate is one of the exceptions. Sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds and all nitrates are soluble.

questions.stem: Which pair of aqueous solutions forms a precipitate when they are mixed together?
questions.explanation: Lead(II) ions and iodide ions form insoluble yellow lead(II) iodide. In each other pair, every possible combination of ions is soluble, so all ions stay in solution.

questions.stem: Which is the net ionic equation for the reaction of lead(II) nitrate solution with potassium iodide solution?
questions.explanation: A net ionic equation shows only the ions that form the precipitate. Pb²⁺ needs two I⁻ to make neutral PbI₂. Potassium nitrate is soluble, so K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions.

questions.stem: Lead(II) nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution. Which are the spectator ions?
questions.explanation: Spectator ions are present before and after the reaction without changing. Pb²⁺ and I⁻ leave the solution as solid PbI₂, while K⁺ and NO₃⁻ remain dissolved.

questions.stem: Copper(II) sulfate solution reacts with sodium hydroxide solution, forming copper(II) hydroxide. Which is the full ionic equation?
options: Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CuOH(s) + Na⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)
questions.explanation: A full ionic equation writes every dissolved ionic compound as separate ions and the precipitate as a solid. Sodium sulfate is soluble, so its ions appear unchanged on both sides, while insoluble Cu(OH)₂ is written as a solid.

questions.stem: Sodium carbonate solution is added to calcium chloride solution. What is the white precipitate?
questions.explanation: Swapping partners gives calcium carbonate and sodium chloride. Most carbonates are insoluble, so CaCO₃ precipitates, while sodium chloride stays dissolved.

questions.stem: Solution X forms a precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution but not with sodium chloride or sodium sulfate solution. Which ion could X contain?
questions.explanation: Magnesium hydroxide is insoluble, while magnesium chloride and magnesium sulfate are soluble. Barium would precipitate with sulfate, silver would precipitate with chloride, and potassium precipitates with none of them.

questions.stem: Which description fits a precipitation reaction?
options: Two ionic solutions mix and an insoluble ionic solid forms
An acid and a base react to form a salt and water
A metal reacts with oxygen and gives out heat and light
One compound breaks down into two simpler substances
questions.explanation: In a precipitation reaction, ions from two solutions combine to form an insoluble compound that separates as a solid. The others describe neutralisation, combustion and decomposition.

questions.stem: In terms of electrons and oxidation state, oxidation is:
options: a gain of electrons, with an increase in oxidation state
a loss of electrons, with a decrease in oxidation state
a gain of electrons, with a decrease in oxidation state
a loss of electrons, with an increase in oxidation state
questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons, so the species becomes more positive and its oxidation state rises. Reduction is gain of electrons and a fall in oxidation state.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation state of manganese in potassium permanganate, KMnO₄?
questions.explanation: K is +1 and each O is −2, so +1 + Mn + 4(−2) = 0 and Mn = +7. The −1 is the charge on the whole MnO₄⁻ ion, not the oxidation state of manganese.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation state of nitrogen in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
questions.explanation: Each H is +1 and the ion's total is +1, so N + 4(+1) = +1 and N = −3. Nitrogen has an oxidation state of +5 in the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻.

questions.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s), which species is oxidised?
options: Copper, whose oxidation state falls from +2 to 0
Sulfur, whose oxidation state falls from +6 to +4
Zinc, whose oxidation state falls from +2 to 0
Zinc, whose oxidation state rises from 0 to +2
questions.explanation: Zinc atoms lose two electrons to become Zn²⁺, an increase in oxidation state, so zinc is oxidised. Cu²⁺ gains those electrons and is reduced. Sulfate is a spectator ion and is unchanged.

questions.stem: Magnesium ribbon is placed in silver nitrate solution. Which is the reduction half-equation?
questions.explanation: Reduction is gain of electrons. Silver ions gain electrons to deposit as silver metal, while magnesium, the more reactive metal, is oxidised to Mg²⁺.

questions.stem: The half-equations are Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. Which is the balanced overall equation?
questions.explanation: Electrons lost must equal electrons gained, so the silver half-equation is doubled before adding. Zn + Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Ag balances atoms but not charge (+1 on the left, +2 on the right).

questions.stem: An iron nail is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. What forms?
options: Nothing, as copper is more reactive
questions.explanation: Iron is above copper in the activity series, so it displaces copper: Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu. A pink-brown coating of copper forms on the nail and the blue colour of the solution fades.

questions.stem: Which mixture does not react?
options: Zinc metal in copper(II) sulfate solution
Magnesium metal in dilute hydrochloric acid
Iron metal in silver nitrate solution
Copper metal in zinc sulfate solution
questions.explanation: A metal only displaces a less reactive metal from solution. Copper is below zinc in the activity series, so it cannot give electrons to Zn²⁺ ions.

questions.stem: In the reaction Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂, which species is the oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: Chlorine gains electrons (0 to −1) and is reduced, so it is the oxidising agent: it oxidises bromide ions to bromine. K⁺ is a spectator ion.

questions.stem: In which reaction do oxidation states change?
questions.explanation: Magnesium goes from 0 to +2 and hydrogen from +1 to 0, so this is a redox reaction. In neutralisation, precipitation and the decomposition of CaCO₃ every element keeps its oxidation state.

questions.stem: Which metal reacts vigorously with cold water?
questions.explanation: Potassium is near the top of the activity series and reacts violently with cold water to form potassium hydroxide and hydrogen. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water, zinc needs steam, and copper does not react.

questions.stem: Which metal does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the activity series, so it cannot reduce H⁺ ions to hydrogen gas. Zinc, magnesium and iron all react, releasing hydrogen.

questions.stem: Zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which gas is produced?
questions.explanation: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. The zinc is oxidised and hydrogen ions are reduced to hydrogen gas, which pops with a lit splint. Carbon dioxide forms when acids react with carbonates.

questions.stem: Metal P displaces metal Q from a solution of Q ions, but does not displace metal R from a solution of R ions. What is the order of reactivity?
questions.explanation: P displacing Q shows P is more reactive than Q. P failing to displace R shows R is more reactive than P. So R is the most reactive and Q the least.

questions.stem: In a class experiment, aluminium foil reacts more slowly with dilute acid than zinc does, although secondary sources place aluminium above zinc in the activity series. What is the best explanation?
options: Foil has a smaller surface area than zinc granules, so it reacts more slowly
Aluminium is coated with a thin layer of oxide that protects it from the acid
The secondary sources are wrong, because aluminium is less reactive than zinc
Aluminium forms Al³⁺ ions, which makes its reactions slower than those of zinc
questions.explanation: Aluminium quickly forms a tough, unreactive oxide layer in air, which must be removed before the metal underneath can react. The difference is a limitation of the test, not a sign that the series is wrong.

questions.stem: Why is gold found uncombined in nature, while iron is found in compounds?
options: Gold has a high melting point, so it cannot be oxidised
Gold is so unreactive that it does not combine with oxygen or water
Gold is so dense that it sinks below minerals it could react with
Gold reacts only with acids, which are rarely found in rocks
questions.explanation: Gold is at the bottom of the activity series and does not react with oxygen, water or most acids, so it stays as the element. Iron is more reactive and is found as oxides and other compounds.

questions.stem: Sodium is more reactive than magnesium. Which data support this?
options: Na has an atomic number of 11, and Mg has an atomic number of 12
Na has a density of 0.97 g cm⁻³, and Mg has a density of 1.74 g cm⁻³
Na forms 1+ ions, while Mg forms 2+ ions with more charge to share
Na has a first ionisation energy of 496 kJ mol⁻¹, Mg 738 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: Metals react by losing electrons. Sodium's lower ionisation energy means its outer electron is removed more easily, so it reacts more readily. Atomic number and density do not explain reactivity.

questions.stem: Why do metals with a larger atomic radius and lower electronegativity tend to be more reactive?
options: Their nuclei have fewer protons, so they attract other atoms less strongly
Their outer electrons are closer to the nucleus, so they are shared more easily
Their atoms are heavier, so they collide with other particles with more force
Their outer electrons are held less strongly, so they are lost more easily
questions.explanation: Metal atoms react by giving up their outer electrons. When these are further from the nucleus and more shielded, less energy is needed to remove them, which is also shown by a low ionisation energy and low electronegativity.

questions.stem: The Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, has had a major impact on agriculture because it:
options: made nitrogen fertilisers cheap, greatly raising crop yields worldwide
produced pesticides that kill insects without harming the crops
removed the need to irrigate crops grown in dry regions
made phosphate fertilisers directly from nitrogen in the air
questions.explanation: Ammonia from the Haber process is made into fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate and urea, which have greatly increased food production. Overuse can cause runoff that leads to algal blooms in waterways.

questions.stem: An antacid containing magnesium hydroxide relieves indigestion. Which type of reaction does it undergo with stomach acid?
options: Decomposition, releasing oxygen gas in the stomach
Displacement, with magnesium replacing hydrogen in water
Neutralisation, forming magnesium chloride and water
questions.explanation: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O. The base neutralises excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach. Magnesium chloride is soluble, so no precipitate forms.
